articles.title: Freda Payne Made Time Stand Still
articles.standfirst: At 84, in gold lamé and black lace, she sang nine legends back into a sold-out Los Angeles room, gave thanks to God from the stage, and delivered a triumph.
articles.image_alt: Freda Payne in a rose satin robe with feather cuffs and gold chandelier earrings, smiling beside her son Gregory Abbott Jr. at Catalina Jazz Club
articles.image_credit: Freda Payne with her son, host Gregory Abbott Jr., at Catalina Jazz Club, Los Angeles. Photo by Terry Bryant.
body: One week after her eighty-fourth birthday, Freda Payne walked out at the Catalina Jazz Club in Los Angeles and made time stand still.

That is not a figure of speech. For as long as the show ran, the room stopped being a room on a Saturday night in Hollywood and became something older and softer, a place where the great women of American song were, for a while, present again.
It was an outstanding night. It was the hottest ticket in Hollywood on a weekend when the MTV Video Music Awards had every other camera in Los Angeles, and it deserved every seat in the house.

Payne’s own note, printed on the night’s running sheet, begins the way the evening felt. “Last week on September 19th, was my birthday. I am so blessed to see another year and still be working. I thank God for that.”
## Nine women, one voice

“Freda Payne Portrays and Honors Legendary Ladies of Song” was written and directed by Donald B. Welch, and it is a small masterpiece of a difficult form. Tribute shows usually feel like a museum. Welch built a living room. The idea, Payne said, was his: “He said, Freda, I want you to do this show honoring several ladies.”

The ladies were Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan, Peggy Lee, Gloria Lynne, Dakota Staton, Lena Horne, Nancy Wilson, Dinah Washington and Eartha Kitt. Payne sang for each of them. “All these ladies were some of my favorite singers back when I started wanting to be a professional singer,” she said.
{{photo:gown}}

She opened with “How High the Moon,” Ella Fitzgerald’s signature, and sang “I Wish You Love” for Gloria Lynne, “Body and Soul” for Sarah Vaughan and “Guess Who I Saw Today” for Nancy Wilson. Each one arrived like a letter from an old friend.
## A voice that soothes

Soothing is the word that keeps coming back. Payne’s voice is unhurried and warm, and it works on a room the way a hand works on a shoulder. It is the voice of a woman who has sung for six decades and has nothing left to prove and nothing left to hide.
{{photo:gold}}
She described Sarah Vaughan’s voice the same way, as “like listening to a violin or a viola. Very soothing.” The two singers met, and Payne came to know her. The compliment runs both directions.
## A girl at Idlewild

The number that carried her furthest back was Dakota Staton’s “The Late Late Show.” Payne was sixteen, living in Detroit, and spending summers at Idlewild, the Black resort community in Michigan, where her mother had a cottage.
“My sister and I were allowed to go to the matinees because we couldn’t go to the nightclubs at night,” she said. “We were still in our teens. And I remember her song.”
Sixty-odd years later she sang it from a Hollywood stage, in gold, to a full house. The sixteen-year-old and the legend were in the same room, and the room was lucky to have both.

Dinah Washington, whom Payne met young and feared at first, is the other side of that memory. “I think it’s because I kind of stood up to her,” Payne said of how the older singer came around. “She could tell I was no pushover.” Washington died at thirty-nine.
## A mother and her son

The evening was announced by Payne’s son, Gregory Abbott Jr., who introduced the special guest and then his mother. He did it with the ease of a man who knows the room. She named him twice in conversation afterward, and each time it was plain which credit mattered most to her. “Most important of all too, my son.”
{{photo:portrait}}
## The company

Thomasina Gross opened the show as Eartha Kitt, a portrayal Payne called “spot on,” and it is. In one staged scene Gross sat at a candlelit table with two martinis and a man in a suit, and held the whole room with a stillness that the photographs catch better than any description.
{{photo:table}}

The band was of the first rank. Josh Nelson was musical director at the piano, and Payne called him one of the best. Chris Colangelo played bass, Ricky Woodard saxophone and Marcello Carelli drums. The cast also included actors Terryl DaLuz and Kyrel Jaundoo, with Chuka Aruh and Mi-cha-El Wat as escorts.
## And then, Fever

A thanksgiving is allowed to be glamorous, and this one was. For Peggy Lee, Payne sang “Fever,” and she brought two men up onto the stage to sing it with, on her own birthday weekend, in gold. She was a show-stopping diva, and she looked magnificent.
{{photo:fever}}
## Hollywood came out

Stefanie Powers and Loretta Devine were in the room, along with a good many other familiar faces from the entertainment industry. Nobody came to be seen. They came to see her, and word of the night has been moving through Los Angeles ever since.
{{photo:powers}}

Payne sails at the end of October aboard Holland America, performing on a cruise from Fort Lauderdale to Puerto Rico and back, with Darlene Love and Wayne Newton on the bill. Anyone who can get on that ship should.
She spent Saturday night saying thank you, and Los Angeles spent it saying the same thing back. It was, from first note to last, a triumph.

articles.title: Taylor Swift takes a sixth Video of the Year at the VMAs; Madonna wins seven
articles.standfirst: The 2026 MTV Video Music Awards ran Sunday night from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Snoop Dogg hosted. Madonna opened the show for the first time in twenty-three years.
body: Taylor Swift won Video of the Year at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday night for “The Fate of Ophelia,” her sixth win in the category and a record no other artist has matched. She thanked Dolly Parton from the stage.

Madonna was the evening’s biggest winner with seven awards, among them Artist of the Year for “Confessions II,” the sequel to her 2005 album. She opened the ceremony with her first VMAs performance in twenty-three years, and had arrived the most-nominated artist of the night with thirteen, a career high.
Snoop Dogg hosted from the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles.

Swift also took Best Director for “Opalite” and received the inaugural Artist Director Honors, a category created this year for work that builds connected narratives across a body of work. She premiered the video for “Patient Zero” during the broadcast.
LISA won Best Pop for “Dream,” featuring Kentaro Sakaguchi. Cardi B, featuring Kehlani, won Best Hip-Hop for “Safe.” Nirvana received the Michael Jackson Video Vanguard Award.
Kacey Musgraves performed a tribute to Dolly Parton. Raye, sombr and Teddy Swims performed a tribute to George Michael.
Reported by the Music Desk of Newswire Hollywood and carried here by arrangement. Full coverage, including the red carpet, is at newswirehollywood.com.

articles.title: Yom Kippur 2026 ended Monday night, closing the Ten Days of Repentance
articles.standfirst: The holiest day in the Jewish year began at sundown on Sunday, September 20 and ended at nightfall on Monday, September 21. It is observed with a fast of roughly 25 hours.
articles.byline: the Gospel Desk, Gospel News Access
body: Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement and the holiest day of the Jewish year, began at sundown on Sunday, September 20, 2026 and ended at nightfall on Monday, September 21.

The day closes the Ten Days of Repentance, the period that opened with Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, which this year began at sundown on Friday, September 11 and ran through the evening of Sunday, September 13. Together Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are known as the High Holy Days, and the days between them are also called the Days of Awe.

Yom Kippur is observed with a fast of roughly 25 hours — no food and no drink from before sundown until after nightfall the following day — and with extended prayer in synagogue. The themes of the day are repentance, atonement and forgiveness: the turning of a person toward God and toward the people they have wronged. The observance is set out in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 16 and Leviticus 23, which appoint the tenth day of the seventh month as a day of atonement and of self-denial.
Because the Jewish calendar is lunisolar, the date moves against the civil calendar each year. In the Hebrew reckoning the day that has just passed was Yom Kippur of the year 5787.

A note for our readers on why this is in a gospel newspaper: Yom Kippur is a Jewish holy day, kept by the Jewish community, and Gospel News Access reports it as what it is rather than as a borrowed occasion. Christian readers may recognise the Day of Atonement as the image the New Testament letter to the Hebrews reaches for when it writes about a single sacrifice and a high priest entering the holy place. That is a point about two texts and the relationship between them. It is not a claim about how anyone observed this week, and it is not an invitation to treat someone else's holy day as a figure of speech.

Gospel News Access has not reported that any gospel artist, church or denomination marked Yom Kippur 2026, because we have not sourced such an observance. Where we can source one, we will report it and name it.
Sources for the dates and the practices in this report: Hebcal's Jewish calendar, Chabad.org, Reform Judaism and the Jewish Virtual Library entries for Yom Kippur 5787.

articles.title: The 41st Stellar Awards are still airing across the country, and the Doves are two weeks out
articles.standfirst: Lisa Knowles-Smith took five. Darrel Walls took Artist of the Year. The broadcast syndication window runs through September 27, and the 57th GMA Dove Awards follow on October 6 with a Richard Smallwood tribute.
articles.byline: the Gospel Desk, Gospel News Access
body: If you have not seen the 41st Annual Stellar Gospel Music Awards yet, you have not missed them. The ceremony was taped on Saturday, August 15, 2026 at the Spectrum Center in Charlotte, North Carolina, and it is still working its way across the country: after premiering on The Stellar Network on August 29 and on BET on August 30, the show went into national broadcast syndication from September 5 through September 27. That window is open right now. Air dates and times vary by market, so the listing to check is your own local station's.
Kirk Franklin hosted. The theme was "Feels Like Home."

The night belonged to Lisa Knowles-Smith, who won five awards — four of them for "Revival: Live in Dallas," recorded with The Brown Singers. She took the Albertina Walker Female Artist of the Year award; Duo/Chorus/Group of the Year and Quartet of the Year with The Brown Singers; Producer of the Year alongside Frederick Perry; and Song of the Year for "Promises (Live)," which she wrote under her given name, Alescia Knowles-Smith. For a group with the history the Brown Singers have, five trophies in one night is a career marker, and it was widely reported as a first for them at this scale.
Darrel Walls won Artist of the Year and Contemporary Male Artist of the Year, both for "Heart of Mine" — the same record that opened his year with a Grammy for Best Gospel Album.

Vincent Bohanan & SOV won three, including Album of the Year for "Live in New York," with further wins in the choir categories. Jonathan McReynolds, John P. Kee and Jekalyn Carr each won more than once — McReynolds for "Still (Live)" featuring Jamal Roberts, Kee for "Throwback: An Evening With John P. Kee Part I," and Carr for "Jekalyn X The Legends." In the hip-hop categories, Lecrae won Rap/Hip Hop Gospel Album of the Year for "Reconstruction" and JustCordell won Rap/Hip Hop Song of the Year for "Movin."
Two honours were given outside the competitive categories. Tasha Cobbs Leonard received the Aretha Franklin Icon Award. Pastor Mike Jr. received the Thomas A. Dorsey Most Notable Achievement Award.

WHAT IS NEXT: the 57th Annual GMA Dove Awards are on Tuesday, October 6, 2026 at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville. The broadcast airs on TBN and the TBN+ app on Friday, October 9 at 7:30 p.m. and 10 p.m. Eastern, simulcast on SiriusXM The Message.

The Doves have announced a tribute to Richard Smallwood featuring Jonathan McReynolds, Kierra Sheard and Donald Lawrence, together with original members of Smallwood's ensemble Vision — among them Maurette Brown Clark and Ted Winn — with Percy Bady as musical director. Tasha Cobbs Leonard is among the announced performers. Anthony Brown, CeCe Winans and Lisa Knowles-Smith are among the announced presenters.

Knowles-Smith arrives in Nashville holding her first two Dove nominations: Traditional Gospel Recorded Song of the Year for "Promises," and Traditional Gospel Album of the Year for "Revival: Live in Dallas." Five Stellars in August and a first Dove nomination in October is the kind of run that usually reshapes a touring calendar.

How this was sourced: the Stellar winners and ceremony details are drawn from the Gospel Music Association (gospelmusic.org), Billboard's published winners list, the Stellar Awards' own site and the Journal of Gospel Music. The Dove Awards date, venue, broadcast details, performers and presenters are drawn from the Gospel Music Association's announcements and Bridgestone Arena's event listing. Gospel News Access did not attend either ceremony and does not report as though it did.

articles.title: Last call: the 41st Stellar Awards leave broadcast syndication on Sunday
articles.standfirst: The syndication window that has carried the ceremony across local stations since September 5 closes September 27. If it has not aired in your market yet, this weekend is the end of the run.
articles.byline: the Gospel Desk, Gospel News Access
body: The 41st Annual Stellar Gospel Music Awards close their national broadcast syndication run on Sunday, September 27. The window opened on September 5, and for three weeks local stations have been slotting the ceremony into their own schedules — which is why it has aired on different nights in different cities, and why some markets are only getting to it now.
If you have been meaning to watch it, this is the weekend. Air dates and times vary by market, so the only reliable listing is your own local station's.

The ceremony was taped on Saturday, August 15, 2026 at the Spectrum Center in Charlotte, North Carolina. Kirk Franklin hosted. The theme was "Feels Like Home." It premiered on The Stellar Network on August 29 and on BET on August 30 before entering syndication.

WHAT YOU ARE WATCHING FOR: Lisa Knowles-Smith won five awards, four of them for "Revival: Live in Dallas" with The Brown Singers — the Albertina Walker Female Artist of the Year award, Duo/Chorus/Group of the Year and Quartet of the Year with The Brown Singers, Producer of the Year with Frederick Perry, and Song of the Year for "Promises (Live)."

Darrel Walls won Artist of the Year and Contemporary Male Artist of the Year for "Heart of Mine." Vincent Bohanan & SOV won three, including Album of the Year for "Live in New York." Jonathan McReynolds, John P. Kee and Jekalyn Carr each won more than once.

Two honours were given outside the competitive categories: Tasha Cobbs Leonard received the Aretha Franklin Icon Award, and Pastor Mike Jr. received the Thomas A. Dorsey Most Notable Achievement Award.

After Sunday the next date on the calendar is the 57th Annual GMA Dove Awards, on Tuesday, October 6 at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, with the broadcast on TBN and the TBN+ app on Friday, October 9.

How this was sourced: the syndication window, ceremony details and winners are drawn from the Gospel Music Association, Billboard's published winners list, the Stellar Awards' own site and Central City Productions, which distributes the show. Gospel News Access did not attend the ceremony and does not report as though it did. We do not hold a market-by-market broadcast schedule and are not publishing one, because a wrong airtime is worse than none.

articles.title: The gospel world this week: Tasha goes unscripted, Anthony Brown returns, Gaither gets a tribute
articles.standfirst: A 34-track live album out of Atlanta, a seventh record after a three-year silence, and a Nashville red carpet for the Gaither songbook. What actually happened in gospel music this month.
articles.byline: the Gospel Desk, Gospel News Access
body: TASHA COBBS LEONARD went back to Atlanta and did not plan it too tightly. "Tasha Unscripted," released September 11 on Motown Gospel and Capitol Christian Music Group, runs 34 tracks recorded before a live audience — more than a decade of her catalogue revisited, with room left for new arrangements and unrehearsed worship to go wherever it went.

The guest list is close to a census of contemporary gospel: Jonathan McReynolds, Karen Clark Sheard, Kierra Sheard, Israel Houghton, William Murphy, Le'Andria Johnson, Travis Greene, Dante Bowe, Melvin Crispell III, Jonathan Nelson and Lisa Knowles-Smith all appear, along with country singer Mickey Guyton. Her Unscripted Nights tour opened the same day in Charlotte to a sold-out house and its announced routing runs through tonight, having passed through Brunswick, Atlanta, Washington, Dallas, Raleigh and New York.
It has been a long few weeks for Cobbs Leonard. She collected the Aretha Franklin Icon Award at the Stellar Awards in August, and she is among the announced performers at the Dove Awards in October.

ANTHONY BROWN & GROUP THERAPY broke a three-year recording silence on September 18 with "Disclosure," their seventh album, on A Major Entertainment with Tyscot and Fair Trade Services. It is ten songs, produced by David "Glo" Outing II with Brown co-producing, and it moves between urban contemporary grooves and full orchestral ballads rather than picking one.

The lead radio single, "Always Be Good," has climbed into the top five of both the Billboard and Mediabase gospel airplay charts, according to the label's announcement. Pre-orders had been open since August 14.

THE GAITHER SONGBOOK got its own night. "You Are Loved: A Tribute To The Songs Of Bill & Gloria Gaither" was released September 25 on DVD, CD and digital, and Gaither Music marked it with a red carpet screening in Nashville for artists and industry guests. The Gaither catalogue has been a shared inheritance across Southern gospel, Black gospel and country for six decades, and a tribute record is overdue rather than early.

ALSO THIS WEEK: The Edwards Family release "Even Till The End" digitally on September 28. And Brothers of the Heart — Jimmy Fortune, Bradley Walker, Mike Rogers and Ben Isaacs — are on the bill at Eric Clapton's Crossroads Guitar Festival at the Moody Center in Austin on September 26 and 27, which is not where a Gaither Music quartet usually turns up.

ONE THING TO GET RIGHT: a headline moving this week has Kirk Franklin joining the SoundExchange Hall of Fame. The honour is real — SoundExchange recognised Franklin as one of the most-streamed artists across its two decades of administering digital performance royalties, an award whose recipients include Mariah Carey, Billy Joel and Usher, and it was presented to him backstage at HBCU Awarefest at State Farm Arena in Atlanta. It is not news from this week, though: SoundExchange announced it in April 2026. What moved this week was a re-report of it. We are spelling that out because our own wire is carrying the later item, and a reader could reasonably take it for a fresh announcement.

TWO DATES TO KEEP: the 41st Stellar Awards leave broadcast syndication on Sunday, September 27, closing the window that opened on September 5. And the 57th Annual GMA Dove Awards are on Tuesday, October 6 at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, broadcasting on TBN and the TBN+ app on Friday, October 9 at 7:30 and 10 p.m. Eastern, simulcast on SiriusXM The Message. The Doves will carry a tribute to Richard Smallwood featuring Jonathan McReynolds, Kierra Sheard and Donald Lawrence with original members of his ensemble Vision.

One thread worth following: Lisa Knowles-Smith took five Stellars in August, holds her first two Dove nominations next month, and turns up as a guest on "Tasha Unscripted." After a career spent largely outside the spotlight, she is having the kind of year that rearranges a touring calendar.

How this was sourced: release dates, labels, credits, track counts and guest lists are drawn from the artists' and labels' own announcements, Shore Fire Media, Billboard, the Gospel Music Association, Gaither Music and The Urban Music Scene. Chart positions are as stated in the label's announcement and are not our own measurement; the GNA charts are published separately and on their own methodology. The SoundExchange award and its April announcement date are from SoundExchange's own release and the Gospel Music Association. Gospel News Access attended none of these events and does not report as though it did.
